Ribbed sculpin Triglops pingelii exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its adaptation to cold, demersal environments in the North Pacific and Arctic. Field surveys indicate that males attain a maximum recorded total length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters], a size that likely represents an upper limit imposed by resource availability in these high-latitude habitats. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight for males has been estimated at 33.2 grams [Wwi = 33.2 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions calibrated for this species. Such modest body dimensions are typical of the Cottidae, a family in which many species remain relatively small as adults. These morphological limits contrast sharply with the prolonged developmental schedule exhibited by Triglops pingelii under the cold temperatures that characterize its native range.

Embryonic and early larval development proceed very slowly when reared at the low ambient temperatures typical of this species' habitat. At a stable water temperature of 0.4 °C [T = 0.4 °C], the interval from fertilisation to eclosion spans approximately 195 days [ab = approximately 195 days], placing this taxon among the most protracted incubators within the Cottidae. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of just 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves packaged within an egg diameter of about 2.25 millimeters. The lecithotrophic phase following hatching is correspondingly extended, with the yolk-sac larva relying on endogenous nutrition for several additional weeks before the onset of exogenous feeding and the transition to a free-swimming, pelagic larval existence.

The onset of sexual maturation is tightly linked to the attainment of a specific body size and is further modulated by the thermal regime. Females typically reach the total length at puberty of 8.7 centimeters [Lp = 8.7 centimeters], at which point the corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 3.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.8 grams]. The duration required to achieve this size, measured as the time since birth at puberty, is estimated at 1,460 days [tp = 1,460 days] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 0.4 °C [T = 0.4 °C]. This four-year interval to maturity is consistent with the slow growth rates characteristic of high-latitude sculpins. The protracted juvenile phase likely reflects the energetic demands of accumulating sufficient lipid reserves in a seasonally variable feeding environment before the onset of gonadal recrudescence.

Reproductive output in this species reflects a strategy of low fecundity per event coupled with a sustained, albeit slow, reproductive cycle. Field observations of spawning adults indicate that females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with an average clutch size of approximately 0.85 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 0.85 eggs per clutch], a low fecundity that is unusual among marine teleosts and may be related to the large, yolk-rich egg size. The daily reproduction rate derived from these values is intrinsically tied to the cold temperatures of the benthic environment. When this maximum reproductive rate is assessed at a temperature of 0.4 °C [T = 0.4 °C], the resulting annual output is consistent with an iteroparous life-history model in which reproductive effort is spread across many seasons.

Longevity estimates for Triglops pingelii indicate that individuals can survive for up to 2,920 days [am = up to 2,920 days] when maintained at a temperature of 0.4 °C [T = 0.4 °C], corresponding to a maximum lifespan of roughly eight years. This extended lifespan is notable among sculpins and aligns with the slow pace of life typical of cold-water species, where reduced metabolic rates are associated with delayed senescence. The overlap between the age at first reproduction and the total lifespan suggests that most individuals experience multiple breeding seasons. Comparative data from related cottids indicate that the combination of small body size, late maturity, and extended longevity observed in Ribbed sculpin represents a distinctive demographic strategy shaped by the persistent low temperatures and seasonally pulsed food availability of its arctic and subarctic habitats.
